extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, government officials, and military legal advisers dealing with laws of war, military occupation, and captured property
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and principles governing spies, military occupation, captured property, the destruction of private property, military tribunals, and related powers and duties of military authorities during war and occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and gravamen of the offense of spy
rubrics_metrics.description: The gravamen of the offense of the spy is the treachery or deception practiced— the being in disguise or acting under false pretenses. (R.S. §1343 referenced.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons found lurking or acting as spies in or about fortifications, posts, quarters, or encampments of the armies are triable by general court-martial or military commission and on conviction shall suffer death; the essential element is treachery/deception (disguise/false pretenses). Cites R.S. §1343 and Hague Convention 1907.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enemy officer in civilian dress with hostile communications = triable as spy
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the enemy's army arrested while lurking in the State in the disguise of a citizen's dress, shown to have passed for hostile purposes to and from Canada and to have held communication with agents of the enemy and conveyed intelligence, was held amenable to trial as a spy before a military court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual showing of covert communications and hostile passage supports presumption of espionage and trial by military tribunal. Citation: R. 11, 474, Feb., 1865; C. 21529, May 14, 1907, Oct. 20, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separated enemy soldier in disguise seeking to rejoin not necessarily a spy
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier of the enemy separated from his army, wandering about in disguise within our lines seeking opportunity to rejoin his regiment, was held not properly chargeable with the offense of the spy, though punishable for disguise as a violation of the laws of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intent: mere attempt to rejoin one's forces (without treachery to obtain information) may remove the espionage character even if disguised; punishment still available for violation of laws of war. Citation: R. 11, 82, Oct., 1864; G. 21529, May 14, 1907, Oct. 20, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from discovery lurking in or near camp disguised as friendly soldier
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or soldier of the enemy discovered 'lurking' in or near a camp or post, disguised in the uniform or overcoat of a United States soldier, is prima facie a spy and liable to trial as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such disguise creates a presumption of espionage unless rebutted by satisfactory evidence of a venial purpose (e.g., visiting family) that shows no intent to obtain information. Multiple historical orders and opinions cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographing fortifications may be treated as espionage
rubrics_metrics.description: A person taking photographs of fortifications in time of war runs the risk of being treated as a spy, or at least of doing an act forbidden by the law of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest outside military reservation is not trespass; seizure and retention of photographic plates is lawful even without prior public notice prohibiting such photography. Cited opinions: C. 2484 Aug. 1898; 7362 Nov. 28, 1899; 13188 Aug. 23, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to suppress newspapers/publications during occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: The commander of an army in occupation and government of the enemy's country may suppress a newspaper or other publication deemed by him injurious to the public interests in exciting opposition to the dominant authority or encouraging support of the enemy's cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A newspaper may be silenced under the laws of war when it is a powerful agent for exciting opposition; suppression is analogous to silencing a fort or battery of the enemy. Cited: R. 2, 585, June, 1863.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction or injury of private property in battle as consequence of war
rubrics_metrics.description: The destruction or injury of private property in battle or the bombardment of cities and towns must be borne by the sufferers as one of the consequences of war; acts that would embarrass or impede the enemy or cripple him may lawfully be ordered by the commanding general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessities of war justify such acts; safety of the State overrides private loss. Examples include breaking roads, burning bridges, destroying means of subsistence. Case: shell fired on Santiago, Cuba—U.S. not legally responsible. C. 5619, Jan. 5, 1899; 11181, Sept. 12, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary occupation/destruction in time of public danger generally uncompensated
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments may temporarily occupy or even destroy property in times of great public danger when public safety demands it; in such cases governments do not admit a legal obligation to compensate the owner; compensation when made is matter of bounty, not legal right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between takings for public use (constitutionally requiring just compensation) and temporary occupation/destruction under military necessity (no strict legal obligation). C. 14292, Mar. 12, 1903.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to occupy public buildings without compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a state of war exists the right of an army to occupy public buildings without compensation in the territory affected cannot be questioned; 'public buildings' include municipal and State buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occupation for military purposes is permissible without compensation. C. 15318, May 7, 1906; 6076, Sept. 29, 1898; 5457, Dec. 8, 1899.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure and use of transportation and means of communication in military operations
rubrics_metrics.description: A belligerent has the right to take forcible possession of a railway or other means of transportation and to use the same in his military operations; this right extends where several powers cooperating against a common enemy make similar seizure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seizure and use of transport are lawful incidents of military operations; reimbursement may be provided by proper departmental claim. C. 11107, Aug. 19, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captured property jure belli accrues to the United States (subject to statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Captured property of an enemy jure belli ordinarily accrues to the United States; application of this principle may be affected by acts of Congress (e.g., confiscation statutes, Captured and Abandoned Property Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the Civil War statutes such as July 17, 1862 and March 12, 1863 affected disposition: personal property captured often sold and proceeds paid into Treasury subject to claims by parties establishing ownership and lack of giving 'aid or comfort' to rebellion. Cases and opinions cited (R. 18, 511; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Captured enemy property not protected by Fifth Amendment takings clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Property of enemies captured jure belli in a civil war did not belong to the class of property protected by the Fifth Amendment's prohibition against taking for public use without just compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captured enemy property may be treated differently from property seized for public use under constitutional takings doctrine. R. 30, 231, Apr., 1870; C. 10787, July 17, 1901; 11583, Nov. 12, 1901; 15448, Nov. 5, 1903.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recaptured property of loyal owners may be returned free of salvage
rubrics_metrics.description: Property of a loyal owner captured by the enemy and afterwards recaptured by Federal forces may be turned over to him by executive authority, when clearly identified, and generally allowed to be received free from any charge in the nature of salvage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive return is appropriate where identification is clear. Cited opinions: E. 1, 424, 428, 456, Nov. and Dec., 1862; 11, 266, Dec., 1864; 20, 485, Mar., 1866.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/military stores taken from enemy are property of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Military stores taken from the enemy upon capture become the property of the United States, and Congress alone can authorize their sale, transfer, or other disposition; private appropriation by officers or soldiers is a military offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 9th article of war's provision that 'all public stores taken from the enemy shall be secured for the service of the United States' aligns with law of nations and bars private capture for personal benefit. Violations subject to military discipline. R. 2, 41, Feb., 1863; C. 12019, Feb. 8, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limits on delivery of captured property to institutions (e.g., Smithsonian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute authorizing delivery to the Smithsonian (section 5586 R.S.) does not apply to captured military stores; such captured military property is United States property and its disposition rests solely with Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request to assign a small Spanish cannon captured at Santiago to the U.S. Museum was denied under this principle. C. 5033, Sept., 1898; 11131, Oct. 11, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flags and colors taken by the Army are generally those of the enemy; resumption/return depends on original ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 218 R.S. requiring collection of flags taken by the Army is believed to refer to enemy flags; a state/regimental flag captured by enemy and retaken may be returned to the State/regiment if originally belonging to it, but if furnished by the United States it is U.S. property disposable only by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish original ownership to determine if return by executive authority is proper. P. 58, 119, Feb., 1893.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military occupation cannot lawfully alienate immovable property to bind after reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the law of war a government by military occupation has no power to alienate immovable property so as to render such alienation effective after the reinstatement of the former government; similar rule probably applies to grants of franchises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and instructions (G.O. 100, A.G.O., 1863) suggest a victorious army appropriates revenues and sequesters property for government, but alienations by occupier that bind after cessation are generally invalid. C. 5076, Sept. 18; 6437.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War lacks power to permanently alienate public domain of newly acquired territory absent Congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a territory becomes subject to U.S. sovereignty by treaty, the Secretary of War is without power, in the absence of congressional authority, to alienate any part of the public domain, though he may license temporary use during military occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after treaty with Spain and effective control of Porto Rico, Secretary could license temporary use but not permanently alienate lands. C. 6984 Nov., 1898.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation among powers allows furnishing military supplies with reimbursement claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When forces of several States cooperate against a common enemy for a common purpose, one may furnish the other with arms, supplies, transport, etc., in the form of loans, gifts, or sale; reimbursement will be made by proper claim to the proper staff department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for allied or cooperating forces; reimbursement subject to departmental claim procedures. C. 11107, Apr., 19, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking possession of enemy funds in banks during occupation justified
rubrics_metrics.description: The taking possession, by order of the military commander, for the use of the military service of moneys belonging to enemies on deposit in banks of an occupied city, was held an act justified by the strict law of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New Orleans banking deposits taken for military use during occupation. R. 19, 612, May, 1866.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes/duties and military levies during occupation become payable to occupant
rubrics_metrics.description: As a result of military occupation the taxes and duties payable by inhabitants to the former government become payable to the military occupant unless substituted by other rates or modes of contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President acted within powers to order tariff and duties levied in occupied Cuban ports; regulations to administer such levies take effect upon occupation and questions thereunder decided by commanding general. C. 5268, Nov., 1898.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special courts (provost courts) may be appointed where ordinary courts are closed but have limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A military officer commanding in time of war in a region in military occupation, where ordinary courts are closed by exigencies of war, is authorized to appoint a special court or judge (e.g., provost courts); such courts had no jurisdiction of purely military offenses and generally were confined to breaches of the peace and violations of civil ordinances or military regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provost courts served as substitutes for police or municipal courts; they could not impose purely military punishments (forfeiture of pay, etc.) on officers/soldiers. Numerous General Orders and cases illustrate both the scope and limits (e.g., R.2,14; R.6,635).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military government promulgation: commander-made laws are valid within territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that may properly be made a law of a military government, and which is promulgated in any effective way that the supreme military commander sees fit, becomes a valid law of that government and must be obeyed by all persons within the territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commander is not bound by prior municipal procedures for promulgation; the chief commander in occupied territory does not occupy a former civil office and is not bound by its rules. C. 5978, May, 1898.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal laws of conquered country continue except as suspended by occupier
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal laws of a conquered country continue in force during the military occupation by the conqueror, except insofar as their operation is necessarily suspended or affected by his acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a will executed during occupation invalid if not attested per state law; military authority cannot invest devisee against heirs if local law unchanged. R. 19, 474, Mar., 1866.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction of property aiding insurgents may be military necessity without liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the owner of property was holding communication with and forwarding supplies to insurgents, his house was burned; held that as the property was destroyed as a military necessity the United States could not be held pecuniarily responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly applied to destruction of market house where military necessity to prevent lawless acts was established. C. 14972, July 25, 1903; Jan. 27, 1904.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military governor's authority: removal and appointment of local officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The military governor of a hostile city may remove for cause duly elected local officials (e.g., alcaldes) and may appoint others during occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmed in opinions/cases such as C. 5873, Feb. 17, 1899; removal for cause within military government's authority during occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military government's right to collect duties and exactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When military government is maintained within an enemy's country, a military government may collect duties and contributions of money exacted by competent military authority are justified by the law of war and conquest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not question the right to collect such duties; e.g., a military-levied tax on cotton applied to hospital and sanitary purposes was authorized. C. 6138, Apr. 12, 1899; R. 18, 668, Mar., 1866.
